opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we think about a lot. The way I frame it is to look for a few properties together.

First, is there a problem that is fundamental, where solving it would unlock a lot of downstream progress? Protein structure prediction was a great example. Determining a single structure experimentally could take a PhD student years, and structure is so central to biology that a solution would ripple out into drug discovery, enzyme design, and basic science.

Second, is there a clear objective, some way of measuring whether you're getting closer to the answer? AI systems thrive when you can tell them what "good" looks like. In protein folding we had the CASP competition and decades of carefully curated structural data, so we could tell unambiguously whether we were making progress.

Third, is there enough data, or a good simulator, or some way of generating signal? Sometimes the data already exists, like the Protein Data Bank. Sometimes you can generate it, as in games or some areas of mathematics, where you can verify answers formally.

And finally, is the search space combinatorially huge, so that human intuition and brute-force computation both struggle? That's where learned models can really shine, because they can learn the structure of the space and search it much more intelligently.

When you find a domain that hits all four, a root-node problem, a clear metric, a source of signal, and a vast search space, that's where we think AI can have transformational rather than incremental impact. That's why we've been excited about areas like materials science, genomics, fusion, and mathematics. And beyond any single breakthrough, the real goal is to give scientists tools that accelerate the whole process of discovery.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that AI benefits a domain most when three things line up. First, there's a well-defined problem where you can actually tell whether a proposed answer is right, so there's a verification signal you can learn against. Second, there's a large search space, where the bottleneck for humans is not understanding but the sheer number of possibilities to explore. And third, the cost of running an experiment or evaluation in the loop is low enough that the system can iterate many times.

Science is where this shows up most clearly. Take protein structure prediction, or materials discovery, or mathematics. In each case there's a real notion of correctness, whether that's experimental structures, a stable crystal, or a formal proof checker. And the search spaces are enormous. Nobody is going to enumerate the space of possible proteins or compounds by hand. That combination is exactly what these models are good at, and it's why we've seen such fast progress there compared to areas where feedback is slow, noisy, or subjective.

The other dimension I weigh is leverage. If you solve a problem in biology or in energy materials, the downstream impact compounds, because every lab working on drugs or batteries builds on that result. So we try to pick problems that sit at the root of many other problems, rather than ones that are impressive but isolated.

And then the honest caveat is that for a lot of domains the limiting factor isn't the model at all. It's data, it's the ability to run the physical experiment, it's the people in that field being willing to work with the tools. So I think the domains that benefit soonest are the ones where there's already a culture of computation and shared data, and the ones that benefit most in the long run are the ones where we invest in building that infrastructure now.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in terms of where there’s a bottleneck between the information we have and our ability to use it. We might have a lot of data, but making sense of that data—or using it to make a prediction or design an experiment—is incredibly difficult. Those are places where AI can be very useful.

Science is particularly exciting to me because advances there can have effects across so many other domains. If you can help scientists understand biology, discover new materials, or develop better algorithms, you’re giving people tools that can enable many further discoveries.

But it’s not just a question of whether an AI model can perform well on a particular task. Can you validate its predictions? Can someone actually use the result? What is the cost of being wrong? Those questions determine whether a promising capability turns into a real benefit. So I would look for important problems where AI can remove a meaningful bottleneck, and where we have a clear way to test whether it’s helping.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it in terms of where there’s a gap between our ability to collect information and our ability to make sense of it. Science is a good example. We have extraordinary instruments generating enormous amounts of data, but turning those observations into understanding—and then into something useful—is still very difficult.

Biology, medicine, materials science, energy: these are areas where even a small improvement in our ability to predict or design something can have a very large impact. And the benefits can extend beyond the person using the AI system. Discovering a better material or understanding a biological process can enable many other people to make progress.

But I wouldn’t say that every problem in those domains is necessarily an AI problem. You have to ask: What is the bottleneck? Can we measure whether we’ve made progress? And can someone actually use the result? For me, the most promising opportunities are where those things come together—a consequential problem, an approach we can test, and a path from a model’s output to a real-world benefit.
